phases.title: First half — Python foundations
phases.summary: Guided modules first, then loops, functions and the statistics library in plain .py files. Exercises 1 to 6, then Practice 1 to 9. No notebooks and no DataFrames yet.

phases.title: Second half — Notebooks, DataFrames and regression
phases.summary: Work in .ipynb files: load data, clean it, group and merge it, form portfolios, plot them and finish with a regression. Practice 10 to 19.

notebooks.title: Lecture 01 — Loading the data
notebooks.summary: The class data comes as plain csv files in fin400/data/. Every lecture starts the same way: read the file, keep the dates as dates, then check the shape before trusting a single number.

exercises.title: Exercise 1 — Load it and describe what you have
Exercise 2 — Read the range before you read the numbers

notebooks.label: Lecture 01

notebooks.title: Lecture 02 — Distributions: loops, transformations and functions
notebooks.summary: Returns are not normal — they are wide, they have fat tails, and they have both signs. The first tool is a loop that walks a list and builds a new one, and the second is turning that loop into a function so the same tran

exercises.title: Exercise 2 — The loop that logs the whole list

notebooks.label: Lecture 02

notebooks.title: Lecture 03 — Statistics with the statistics library
notebooks.summary: The library only formalises what you can already write with a loop. That matters for one reason: if you cannot write the loop, you do not know what the library is doing.

exercises.title: Exercise 1 — Fix the maximum that returns zero
Exercise 2 — Read a summary before running it

notebooks.label: Lecture 03

notebooks.title: Lecture 04 — Squared deviations, the CDF and the inverse CDF
notebooks.summary: Two ideas that the rest of the course leans on: how far values sit from their mean, and how a normal distribution converts between a value and a probability.
notebooks.label: Lecture 04

notebooks.title: Lecture 05 — A list of CDF values, and looping by index
notebooks.summary: The exercise pattern: given a list of values and a mean and standard deviation, return the probability of each one. One function, one loop, one cdf call per value.
notebooks.label: Lecture 05

notebooks.title: Lecture 06 — Empirical probability and the shape of a strategy
notebooks.summary: "How often does this strategy lose more than 5% in a month?" is not a question about a formula. It is a question about how many months did that — an empirical probability.

exercises.title: Exercise 1 — Where do the months fall?
Exercise 2 — Count before you take a share

notebooks.label: Lecture 06

notebooks.title: Lecture 07 — A first look at pandas: columns, describe, summaries
notebooks.summary: A DataFrame is a table with column names. Three moves cover most of the work: pick a column, make a new column from old ones, and summarise the result.

exercises.title: Exercise 1 — Two new columns and a summary
Exercise 2 — Fill in the quantile call

notebooks.label: Lecture 07

notebooks.title: Lecture 08 — Conditional logic and boolean indexing
notebooks.summary: Filtering is two steps that look like one: build a True/False column, then use it to pick rows. Combination is where it usually goes wrong.
notebooks.label: Lecture 08

notebooks.title: Lecture 11 — Reviewing a data set before you trust it
notebooks.summary: Before any analysis: how many rows, which columns, what type is each one, and are there dates hiding in a string column?
notebooks.label: Lecture 11

notebooks.title: Lecture 12 — groupby: one summary per group
notebooks.summary: groupby is the pandas version of "for each group, compute…". Split, apply, combine.

exercises.title: Exercise 1 — Median age and BMI by gender
Exercise 2 — Fill in the two-key groupby

notebooks.label: Lecture 12
